title: A Glowing Rocket Engine That Could Speed Us to Mars
summary: Imagine an engine that doesn't roar like a rocket but glows white-hot and pushes a spaceship for months. That's what NASA just tested at its Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California. On February 24, engineers fired up a new kind of thruster that runs on lithium metal vapor. It got so hot—over 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit—that its central part glowed bright white. This is not your typical rocket engine. Most rockets burn fuel in a big, loud burst. This one uses electricity to push out a steady stream of glowing plasma (a super-hot gas). It's much more efficient, using up to 90% less fuel. The test reached 120 kilowatts of power. That's more than 25 times the power of the engines on NASA's Psyche spacecraft, which is currently zooming through space. Why does this matter? If we want to send astronauts to Mars, we need engines that can run for a very long time without carrying tons of fuel. This new thruster could be paired with a nuclear power source to make the trip possible. The next step is to make it even more powerful—up to 1 megawatt per engine. A Mars mission might need several of these working together for over 23,000 hours. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said this test shows real progress toward putting an American astronaut on the Red Planet. It's a small but glowing step toward a giant leap.
why_it_matters: This glowing engine could one day power the spaceship that carries the first astronauts to Mars, turning science fiction into reality for your generation.

keywords.explanation: A soft, silvery metal often used in batteries and now being tested as a fuel for rocket engines.
A small engine on a spacecraft that pushes it forward or helps it steer.
A super-hot gas that conducts electricity and glows; it's the stuff stars and lightning are made of.
Getting more out of less — like a car that goes farther on a single tank of gas.

background_read: NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL, a famous space research center in California) has been building and testing spacecraft for decades.
The Psyche spacecraft mentioned is currently flying to a metal-rich asteroid to learn how planets like Earth formed.
To send humans to Mars, we need engines that can push a spaceship for months without carrying huge amounts of fuel — electric thrusters paired with nuclear power could be the answer.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA engineers and administrator Jared Isaacman at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
WHAT: Successfully tested a new electric thruster that glowed white-hot and uses lithium vapor plasma to push with great efficiency.
WHERE: At NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
WHY: To develop an engine that can run for thousands of hours on little fuel, making a future crewed mission to Mars possible.

perspectives.description: They see this as a breakthrough that could make trips to Mars cheaper and more sustainable, opening a new era of deep-space travel.
They worry that using a nuclear power source in space could be dangerous if something goes wrong, and the engine still needs years of testing to be reliable.
They remind everyone that the engine must become much more powerful and survive 23,000 hours of operation — a huge engineering challenge that is far from solved.
